content:
Does Formal Frontier have standards for Palomar-checked formalizations of existing published papers, for example:

  • Formalization Scope. What should be formalized? My practice is to cover all definitions, theorems, examples and factoids in a paper, including ones where the proof is "one may easily see that" or "I will write this down some other time". The latter can lead to proofs that are more modern than the paper. A factoid is an unnumbered claim without proof.
  • Proof content. My practice is to follow the steps of the published proof. For this reason it is concerning to see such a formalization go into a library which has the practice of automatically golfing proofs over time, as this can lead to novel proofs that don't match the original paper. Which there's nothing wrong with that, except that it is not a faithful reproduction.
  • Lean coding practices. My practice is to produce a lint-free result with classes, structures defs in separate self-named files, no file over 1000 lines. I pay close attention to files where the .olean is massive. This tends to happen for capstone theorems and can be mitigated somewhat without changing the original proof.
  • Formalization documentation. It is unclear, especially for arXiv, whether a formalization document is notable/publishable, where it should be published if not arXiv (and if so how to get it indexed in Google Scholar), how much of the formalization process should be documented, especially if it is a human effort, a human-in-the-loop effort, or a purely automated effort. Should the proofs in Lean be decompiled into English and compared with the original proofs? Should the Lean code be printed in the paper or just a pointer to GitHub? How about the statement but not the bodies of theorems? All of structures/class/defs, some or none? An official Formal Frontier template would be really helpful. It is very easy to produce a formalization note which is far longer than the original paper. This question also goes to new mathematics papers that come out of the box with a Lean formalization: How much Lean should be visible in the paper? Here is an example where the practice is to just inline theorem headers.

Palomar requires a #formalization.yaml, which is a standard that was set by the Formal Frontier team.

Does that answer your question?

No. I know how to make a formalization yaml. The questions are about what constitutes a good formalization of a mathematical article (scope and content), what is a good Mathlib-quality Lean coding standard, what would be a palatable template for reporting a signifcant formalization effort, and what is the right Google-Scholar-indexable repository for formalization reports. If this is the wrong channel for these questions, please feel free to move this thread to a better place.

P.S. Side question, if a formalization happened to be in Agda or Isabelle or similar, is that eventually in scope for Palomar or should Agda or Isabelle centric folks make an Agdamar or an Isabellomar?
In that case the answer to your original question is: "No, Formal Frontier does not have such standards".
But should it, or is that out of scope for Formal Frontier?

Lars Ericson said:

  • Formalization Scope. What should be formalized? My practice is to cover all definitions, theorems, examples and factoids in a paper, including ones where the proof is "one may easily see that" or "I will write this down some other time". The latter can lead to proofs that are more modern than the paper. A factoid is an unnumbered claim without proof.

There are a lot of edge cases here.

  • Presumably things called "lemma", "proposition", "corollary" etc. all count as theorems?
  • Papers may also contain statements from the existing literature in an introduction. Probably those don't count since it's only things the paper is claiming as one of its own results (whether or not new) that should be in a formalization of that paper? An introduction is also likely to simplify statements from the literature rather than giving them in fully precise form. It might also have "one may easily see that" variants that don't actually themselves appear in the prior literature.
  • When are claims appearing in the middle of a proof meant to be formalized as their own statements? If you follow the steps of the published proof that tends to follow automatically, given that good Lean practice involves much smaller lemmas than informal mathematics (and people can sometimes cite results from the middle of a proof, not just something appearing as a standalone result in another paper).

And several more when a paper has computational elements, which in some cases can blur the lines between proof-based mathematics and mathematics as an experimental science.

  • A paper could be mainly non-computational, or mainly use only small-scale computations that can be formalized - but also present information about results of larger computations that are too large to formalize.
  • If the paper says "a search up to N found that X is the smallest counterexample, and the only one up to N, to conjecture Y", is a formalization only meant to formalize that X is a counterexample to conjecture Y, which might be trivial, or also to formalize that it's the smallest counterexample, and the only one up to N, which might be infeasible?
  • What about informal descriptive statements (possibly about the observed results of computations) which might not have a precise formal meaning at all? If results of a computation are presented graphically, is that meant to be turned into a formal statement about the points plotted? If a numerical value of a constant appearing in a proof is given, are all the decimal places given meant to be formally proved correct, not just whatever bounds are needed by the proof?

@Joseph Myers for Palomar there can't be any admits or sorrys or axioms. A paper may cite existing literature in an instance where Mathlib hasn't developed that math, in which case the supporting paper's proof needs to be brought in and formalized to support its use.

Lemma, proposition, corollary all count and need to be formalized to complete a proof without holes.

For "I will write this down some other time", I had a specific example in mind (see page 78):

The author has obtained an extension of Theorem 4.1 to infinite Boolean algebras by using the Hahn-Banach Theorem in the same way that it was applied in Kelley (1959), where the problem of the existence of strictly positive measures was solved. If the result proves to be of interest, it will be published in a future paper.

This is what I call a factoid (unnumbered but trusted theorem with no supplied proof). The proof for this was, per our literature search, novel, required some structures that we didn't immediately find in Mathlib for universal realizations of a Boolean algebra and generalized Kelley cover, and comprised about 800 lines of Lean 4 code.
